raw_context: Viral meme from Claudine Barretto's Instagram videos where she repeatedly cut herself off mid-sentence while thanking sponsors; became a goldmine of relatable meme content on TikTok, Twitter, and Facebook in 2024

Used in meme captions: 'Ang boogsh ng party ni Maria, ang daming ilaw!' — describes something extravagant or over-the-top; modern evolution of 'bongga' popularized on Filipino Facebook meme pages 2024-2025
Used in Filipino social media comments: 'Ang ganda ng outfit mo, sobrang estetik!' — describes someone or something as visually appealing or aesthetic; trending on Filipino IG and meme pages 2024

From Filipino internet culture: 'Huwag masyadong dogshow, baka magalit siya!' — the practice of making satirical jokes or memes about a person or public figure; defined on multiple Filipino slang reference sites 2024

Filipino meme and social media usage: 'Dasurv mo yan!' — Filipinized spelling/pronunciation of 'deserve'; used sincerely or sarcastically when someone gets what they deserve; circulating on Facebook meme groups 2024-2025

Viral social media phrase: used to over-dramatize mundane situations for comedic effect, e.g. 'Na para bang ikaw na ang best cook sa mundo pag nag-fry ka ng itlog' — found new life in Filipino meme pages and Twitter 2024-2025

Disaster humor meme trend: Filipinos defying typhoons and floods with humor; trend resurfaces every typhoon season on Filipino Facebook and TikTok; viral around Typhoon Carina (July 2024) coverage on Spot.ph

Filipino internet phrase: 'Alam na this' — implies shared knowledge or mutual understanding without needing to explain; used in meme captions and group chats to signal everyone already knows what's happening; widely documented in 2024 Filipino slang guides

Filipino exclamation: 'Naks, may boyfriend na pala!' — a playful mock-admiration or teasing reaction, like 'Ooooh!' or 'Look at you!'; used sincerely or sarcastically in meme comments and captions; resurgent in Filipino meme pages 2023-2025

Visayan expletive adapted into meme culture: 'Yawa ka talaga!' — literally 'devil' in Visayan; used humorously to call out trolls, rascals, or relatable struggle; widely used in Filipino meme pages especially with Visayan crossover humor 2023-2025

Filipino term of endearment in meme captions: 'Beh, grabe yung nangyari kanina!' — used between close friends, equivalent to babe/sis/bro; common in Filipino Facebook group chats and meme comment sections 2023-2025

Softener/joke marker from Filipino gay lingo now mainstream: 'Crush ko na siya forever. Chos!' — appended at end of sentence to signal joking or lightening a bold statement; ubiquitous in Filipino Facebook meme captions 2023-2025

From comedian Vice Ganda and noontime show It's Showtime segment 'Pak Ganern' (2016); means 'on point / nailed it / that's how it's done'; from 'tumpak' (correct) + 'ganoon' (like that); still heavily used in Filipino meme pages 2023-2025: 'Yes gurl, pak awra!'

Scrambled form of 'malupet/malupit' (extreme/exceptional): 'That performance was so petmalu!' — used to describe something beyond cool or extraordinary; born from Filipino internet culture's love of word scrambling; still used in meme captions 2023-2025

Filipino slang for romantic partner: 'May jowa ka na ba?' (Do you have a boyfriend/girlfriend?) — used in meme templates and hugot meme pages; one of the most commonly used terms in Filipino online relationship humor 2023-2025

Phonetic Tagalog slang for 'iyan' (that): 'Parang ganyan yarn eh' — used by appending to end of words or sentences; found in Filipino internet slang guides and meme comment sections; documented on The Smart Local PH 2024
Shortened 'best friend' used as term of address in meme captions: 'Bes, tingnan mo to!' — common in Filipino Facebook meme groups and group chats; blends with bekimon culture; widely used 2023-2025
